title: Brooklyn's Preseason Roll Hides Familiar Defensive Flaws
author: Max
summary: The Nets are 3-0, but their 131-122 win over Washington suggests offense alone won't be enough once the games count.

content.value:
## The Shooting Touch Keeps Coming

Brooklyn improved to 3-0 in preseason with a 131-122 win over Washington on Monday night at Capital One Arena, and the offensive firepower that carried them through their first two exhibitions showed up again. The Nets converted 29 of 40 two-point attempts for 72 percent, a ridiculous mark even in October basketball. Michael Porter Jr. led the way with 22 points after missing the second preseason game with wrist soreness, and the Nets finished shooting 56.8% from the field with 17 threes and 50 points in the paint.

That's real firepower. Porter has been the story of this preseason run—he dropped 22 on 8-of-13 shooting, with a block and two steals thrown in. The fit alongside Julius Randle looks legitimate. Porter scored 13 points on five-of-six shooting in just seven minutes during the first quarter, picking defenses apart before they could settle. When your small forward can get going like that while your power forward facilitates, you have something to work with.

But offense was never Brooklyn's big question mark. The concern walking into this season was whether a team with this much question mark in its interior defense could keep anyone in front of them. Monday's result offered zero comfort on that front.

## Defense Remains a Glaring Issue

Defense was optional in the first half: the two teams combined for 145 points, and both shot 50% from deep. When both teams are lighting it up like that, you're not playing defense—you're playing track meet basketball. The Wizards trailed just 73-72 at halftime, which tells you everything about Brooklyn's inability to get stops when it mattered.

Washington isn't a juggernaut. This is a rebuilding franchise trotting out a mix of young players trying to prove themselves. Kyshawn George paced the Wizards with 21 points, Bilal Coulibaly finished with 19 points on 7-for-11 shooting, and Bub Carrington added 14 with three triples. Brooklyn let Washington hang around all night: the Nets scored just five points in the first four and a half minutes of the second half and fell behind 82-78, and the Wizards hit 27 of 29 at the line even with Trae Young shooting 1-of-5 and coughing it up eight times.

You can't win games 131-122 in the regular season and expect to contend for anything. This was a preseason game where rotations are loose and effort varies, but the pattern is unmistakable. Brooklyn has no defensive identity right now, and coach Jordi Fernández has his work cut out for him trying to install one before the games count.

## Young Talent Flashed, Turnovers Lingered

Nolan Traoré gave the second unit a real lift off the bench, and it's easy to see him as the backup point guard Fernández needs. Noah Clowney, quiet in the first half, finished with 15 points and hit four of his six threes. That's the kind of spark Brooklyn needs from its young core—energy, shooting, and a willingness to attack—and production like that earns minutes.

But the sloppiness remains a problem. Brooklyn gave the ball away roughly 18 times, 10 of them in the second half. You can chalk some of that up to youth and unfamiliarity, but turnovers have been a theme all preseason. When you're trying to outscore teams rather than outdefend them, you can't afford to hand opponents extra possessions. Washington capitalized, and in tighter games against better opponents, those mistakes will be fatal.

Grant Nelson scored nine points in the fourth quarter and grabbed four boards in 8:51 of action, showing the kind of two-way energy that could earn him real minutes. The depth is there if Brooklyn wants to tap into it, but depth only matters if the foundation is sound.

## The Wins Mean Nothing Without Substance

Brooklyn is 3-0. That's nice. It beats going 0-3 and dealing with panic before the season even starts. But these games mean nothing if the Nets can't figure out how to defend when it counts. It's only preseason, sure, but the defensive habits you build in October are the ones that show up in November.

Porter and Randle can score. That much is clear. But championship teams—hell, *playoff* teams—defend at a level Brooklyn hasn't approached yet. Fernández has one preseason game left, Wednesday in Miami, to install a system that works, to convince his players that effort on that end matters, and to find lineups that don't hemorrhage points every time the other team runs a pick-and-roll.

Right now, the Nets look like a team that can score 115 points a night and lose by six. That's not a recipe for success. It's a recipe for a long winter in Brooklyn.
